articles.title: China's using clean tech to shape global climate fight, growth
articles.summary: Beijing/Washington DC/London: China sent $132 billion in clean technology and investment to the developing world last year, by far the largest
articles.body: Beijing/Washington DC/London: China sent $132 billion in clean technology and investment to the developing world last year, by far the largest contribution to carbon-dioxide reduction of any country. In fact, the nation's green-manufacturing juggernaut, built in part through heavy subsidies from Beijing, nearly matches the current total of grants, loans and private finance that all wealthy countries sent to poorer ones in 2024 to help fight climate change, according to a Reuters analysis.The total included clean-tech exports and an estimated $40 billion in Chinese FDI in clean-tech projects in developing countries, based on data compiled by researchers at London School of Economics. It nearly matched the $137 billion in climate finance wealthy nations provided poorer countries in 2024 under UN pledges, according to OECD.The figures are not directly comparable. China's contribution comprises commercial clean-energy transactions, while climate finance also supports areas such as climate-resilient agriculture and recovery from disasters. Most global climate finance takes the form of loans, a 2024 Reuters investigation found.Reuters calculated Chinese clean-tech exports using customs data for countries OECD classifies as developing. Once deployed, last year's exports will help Global South avoid 257 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually, equal to France's yearly CO2 emissions, according to Lauri Myllyvirta, co-founder of Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. This year's exports are on track to avoid 337 MtCO2 there.China remains the world's biggest greenhouse-gas emitter because of its population, heavy industry and reliance on coal. However, subsidies that helped it dominate solar panels, batteries, electric vehicles and wind turbines have also made it a major force in cutting emissions.Li Shuo, head of China Climate Hub at Asia Society Policy Institute, said China's manufacturing boom offered another pathway beyond rich-country finance: lowering clean-technology prices through innovation and scale until developing countries adopt it for economic reasons. "You can align it to your economic agenda," he said. Beijing has shown little interest in turning commercial strength into diplomatic leadership since Trump withdrew the US from international climate cooperation in 2025.China's manufacturing scale has meanwhile made renewable energy cheaper across the developing world. Ethiopia banned combustion-engine car imports in 2024 largely to reduce its fuel import bill. Pakistan imported 17 GW of Chinese solar last year, roughly matching Germany's installations that year. Nearly two-thirds of China's solar-panel exports and the cells used to make them went to developing countries. ReutersYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Chhattisgarh man kills cousin's 4-year-old son, removes kidneys, lungs and eyes; keeps organs in bucket
articles.summary: RAIPUR: A 27-year-old farm worker allegedly killed his cousin’s four-year-old son and removed organs from his body in Chhattisgarh’s Jashpur district,
articles.body: RAIPUR: A 27-year-old farm worker allegedly killed his cousin’s four-year-old son and removed organs from his body in Chhattisgarh’s Jashpur district, police said, claiming he conceived the plan while browsing social media for ways to make quick money.Basudev alias Tangnu, a resident of Chalni Gorrapath village, was arrested on Sunday after the child’s body was found concealed in a sack in a water-filled pit in Sanna village. Police said they recovered a bucket containing body parts, a knife, a shovel and his mobile phone.The purported motive rests on the accused’s statement during interrogation. Police have not disclosed evidence of contact with prospective buyers or any organ sale.According to police, Basudev stated during interrogation that after killing the child, he cut open the chest and abdomen with the same knife and removed a kidney, a lung and an eye, placing them in a plastic bucket.He then wrapped the body in a blanket and quilt, stuffed it into a sack and partly buried it in a water-filled pit in a field.Police said he separately concealed the bucket containing the body parts, along with the knife and a shovel, in a pit near a bamboo thicket.The child, Jitendra Ram, went missing on November 5. His father, Ramjeet Ram, 36, had moved to Sanna with his family about a year ago for work and lived in a hut near the Aamatchua river dam. Basudev, Ramjeet’s maternal cousin, frequently visited their home.According to the father’s complaint, Basudev took him and another acquaintance out for drinks around 9am on November 5. They later went towards the bus stand while Basudev left separately. When Ramjeet returned home, his son was missing. A witness told him he had seen the boy accompanying Basudev towards a hut in a field.After searching nearby villages and fields, Ramjeet and his relatives found the child’s body on November 7. It was wrapped in bedding, stuffed into a sack and partly covered with soil in a pit near a maize field.Police said Basudev, who grew vegetables on a farmer’s land and lived in a hut there, was dissatisfied with his earnings. During questioning, he purportedly told investigators that searching social media for ways to earn more had given him the idea of selling children’s organs.Investigators said he lured Jitendra away, took him to several places and later bought liquor and chicken. He allegedly gave the child alcohol and killed him with a knife after he fell asleep. articles.title: ‘Some days better than others’: Joe Biden’s memoir promotion to be limited amid cancer battle
articles.summary: Former US President Joe Biden has said his battle with prostate cancer will limit the number of promotional appearances he can make for his upcoming
articles.body: Former US President Joe Biden has said his battle with prostate cancer will limit the number of promotional appearances he can make for his upcoming memoir, "Promise Me, America", which is due to be released on November 17.“Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down,” Biden, 83, wrote on social media on Sunday. He said he would not be able to take part in as many conversations about the book as he had hoped, but added that he was hopeful “the words on the page speak for themselves”.Biden’s publisher announced the memoir on July 15. The book is described as his personal account of his four years in the White House, covering his presidency, his decision to seek a second term and his eventual withdrawal from the 2024 presidential race.The 480-page memoir is expected to cover his administration’s response to the Covid-19 pandemic, the January 6 Capitol attack, the economy, infrastructure and healthcare, as well as US foreign policy and its support for Ukraine. It will also offer Biden’s account of the decision to step aside from the presidential contest. The title echoes his 2017 memoir, Promise Me, Dad, which focused on the death of his son Beau.Biden's health has remained a concern since he disclosed his prostate cancer diagnosis in May 2025, less than four months after leaving office. His office said the cancer had a Gleason score of 9, indicating an aggressive form of the disease, and had already spread to his bones. It also said the cancer appeared to be hormone-sensitive, making it possible to manage with treatment.Biden underwent radiation therapy and hormone treatment. In September 2026, he said the radiation treatment had “worked as intended” and that his doctors had helped bring the disease under control. He did not say he was cancer-free.However, his son Hunter Biden offered a account of his condition in an interview with the BBC in August. He said the cancer had “metastasized into his bones and further”, describing it as painful and debilitating.“It’s really sad to watch,” Hunter said, adding that he wished his father would “complain more” about his health because “it’s not good”.Biden, who turns 84 on November 20, said when the memoir was announced in July that he had been spending time with his family and receiving treatment for cancer. “I’m dealing with a cancer diagnosis, been getting treatment, and it’s going really well,” he said at the time.You use AI every day. articles.body: US secretary of state Marco Rubio had warned senior Trump administration officials about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's alleged ties to a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working for Beijing's intelligence agency, months before the company launched an independent investigation into the matter.Rubio oversaw the drafting of a highly classified memo circulated among senior administration officials during the spring, warning that Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, whom American intelligence agencies believed had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, The New York Times reported.The memo was based on intelligence gathered through electronic surveillance targeting Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and senior executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed. US officials suspected the company was involved in illegally smuggling restricted Nvidia semiconductors into mainland China.The revelations have now prompted Nvidia's board of directors to launch an independent investigation into reports that its chief executive was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The company formally announced the inquiry on Sunday, saying a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, would examine all available information.The board said it had "no reason to believe" that either US national security or Nvidia's trade secrets had been compromised. It added that Huang fully supported the review and had committed to cooperating with the investigation.In a letter to employees, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and colleagues, saying he took "full responsibility" for his actions. He did not name Alice Huang or directly address her alleged links to Beijing."I love our country and our company," Huang said, adding that he was committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security.US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, praised the Nvidia chief executive when asked about the allegations. Trump said he had not spoken to Huang about the latest developments but described him as an "honourable guy" who had done an "amazing job" for the country.Asked whether he regretted not acting on intelligence briefings about the alleged espionage operation, Trump again defended Huang, saying he probably had an explanation for the situation.Huang, 63, will remain at the helm of Nvidia while the investigation is underway. articles.title: Princess Margaret received a 10-acre Caribbean plot as a wedding gift; the secluded Mustique villa she built there now welcomes guests for up to $50,000 a week
articles.summary: Princess Margaret, the younger sister of Queen Elizabeth II, received a 10-acre plot on the Caribbean island of Mustique as a wedding present in 1960 from
articles.body: Princess Margaret, the younger sister of Queen Elizabeth II, received a 10-acre plot on the Caribbean island of Mustique as a wedding present in 1960 from British aristocrat Colin Tennant, later Lord Glenconner. She subsequently commissioned renowned British designer Oliver Messel to build a private holiday residence on the property, naming it Les Jolies Eaux, meaning 'beautiful waters'. The villa became one of Margaret's favourite retreats, where she spent holidays and entertained friends away from royal engagements and public attention. More than six decades later, the former royal residence is available for luxury holiday rentals. Located on a secluded stretch of Mustique's southern coastline, the five-bedroom property commands rates of up to $50,000 per week during the January-April high season.Princess Margaret's 10-acre wedding gift on MustiqueThe story of Les Jolies Eaux began with Colin Tennant, a Scottish aristocrat who purchased Mustique in the late 1950s for approximately £45,000. He envisioned transforming the relatively undeveloped island into an exclusive residential retreat for friends, wealthy visitors and members of the international elite.In 1960, following Margaret's marriage to photographer Antony Armstrong-Jones, Tennant offered her a choice between a conventional wrapped present and a piece of his Caribbean island. Margaret chose the land, receiving a 10-acre plot on a private peninsula towards the southern end of Mustique.She first visited the island during her honeymoon Caribbean cruise aboard the Royal Yacht Britannia. The property offered a secluded setting where she could spend time away from the formal responsibilities associated with royal life.Oliver Messel designed Princess Margaret's Caribbean villaMargaret commissioned Oliver Messel, a celebrated British theatrical and film designer, to create the residence. Messel was also the uncle of her husband, Antony Armstrong-Jones, later Lord Snowdon. He became one of the principal architects associated with Mustique's distinctive residential style.The villa was designed around an open courtyard, with buildings arranged to take advantage of the tropical surroundings and sea views. Its architectural features included coral stone, airy interiors, covered outdoor spaces and a swimming pool surrounded by landscaped gardens.Construction began in the late 1960s, and the residence was completed in the early 1970s. It was named Les Jolies Eaux, a French expression meaning 'beautiful waters'.Margaret also took a personal interest in its interiors. In an interview published in Architectural Digest in October 1979, she explained that Messel had drawn the house while she handled the decorating. She wanted the interiors to reflect her own ideas about comfort and intimate living spaces.The residence featured blue-and-white decorative elements, patterned fabrics, porcelain plates and personal objects. Her bedroom, notably, was decorated in bright orange. A portrait of Queen Elizabeth II was also displayed inside the house.Inside Les Jolies Eaux: Five bedrooms, a private pool and Caribbean viewsThe villa occupies a secluded position at the southern tip of Mustique, overlooking the Caribbean Sea. Its landscaped grounds extend towards Gelliceaux beach, giving the property direct access to a quiet coastal setting.According to the Mustique Company's official listing, the residence has five bedroom suites and can accommodate up to 10 guests. Its principal features include:A Great Room opening towards the swimming pool and gardens.Five bedrooms with en-suite bathrooms.A private plunge pool.An open-sided dining pavilion beside the pool.Extensive lawns and landscaped tropical gardens.A home office and outdoor entertaining spaces.A children's bunkroom available on request for an additional charge.The property's layout combines indoor living spaces with open-air areas designed to make the most of the tropical climate. Its gardens and position near the coastline are among the features highlighted in the official rental description.The villa became part of Princess Margaret's personal historyMustique became an important destination in Margaret's personal life, and she reportedly visited Les Jolies Eaux twice a year for much of her adult life. The island offered privacy and an informal environment in which she could spend time with friends away from Britain.The property also became associated with a widely publicised episode in her marriage. In 1976, photographs of Margaret with landscape gardener Roddy Llewellyn were published in British newspapers. The pictures were taken during their time together on Mustique and attracted considerable media attention.Margaret and Lord Snowdon had already been experiencing marital difficulties and had separated before the photographs appeared. Their divorce was finalised in 1978.The episode brought further attention to Mustique, reinforcing its image as a private Caribbean destination frequented by prominent personalities.Princess Margaret's former villa now rents for up to $50,000 a weekThe former royal residence is now available as a luxury holiday rental through the Mustique Company. Its weekly price varies according to the season, with the January-April period carrying the higher rate.The Mustique Company's official rental listing advertises a weekly rate of $35,000 for stays between May 1 and December 18, 2026, rising to $50,000 per week for the January 4 to April 30, 2027 season.The listed prices are subject to an 11% government tax and a 12% island fee. A discretionary staff gratuity of 5%-10% is also recommended. Flights, food and beverages are charged separately.The villa comes with a dedicated team comprising a butler, chef, gardener and two housekeepers. Guests can therefore access hospitality services alongside the privacy of an independently rented residence.The five-bedroom property accommodates up to 10 guests, with a children's bunkroom available for an additional charge.Mustique developed into an exclusive Caribbean retreatMustique's transformation into an exclusive holiday destination began under Colin Tennant, who purchased the island in 1958 and invested in infrastructure, roads and residential development. The Mustique Company was subsequently established to oversee the island's development and manage its properties.The island attracted wealthy visitors, celebrities and members of royal families, partly because of its emphasis on privacy and limited commercial development. Musicians and public figures, including Mick Jagger, have also been associated with Mustique.Its residential landscape includes villas designed by architects and designers such as Oliver Messel, whose work helped establish the island's distinctive architectural identity. Les Jolies Eaux remains among its best-known properties because of its connection to Princess Margaret and its history as a former royal residence.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Her grandparents bought 146 acres in South Carolina in the 1940s; she promised her mother she would keep it together and has now barred future development on the family land
articles.summary: A woman in South Carolina has permanently protected her family's 146-acre property from future development, fulfilling a promise she made to her mother.
articles.body: A woman in South Carolina has permanently protected her family's 146-acre property from future development, fulfilling a promise she made to her mother. Alice Smith placed the land, known as Duck Haven, in Pickens County under a conservation easement, a legal arrangement that restricts future construction while allowing the family to retain ownership.According to a report by WVLT 8, Smith's grandparents bought the property in the 1940s. She wanted to ensure that the land, which had remained with the family for generations, would not be sold or taken over for development. She said she had promised her mother that she would find a way to keep the property together. "I made a promise to my mother that I would find a way to keep the land together," Smith said as quoted by WVLT 8.The 146-acre property has rolling fields that connect to the Saluda River. It was mostly farmland when her grandparents purchased it, according to Smith. By choosing a conservation easement instead of accepting development offers, she has ensured that restrictions on future development will remain in place even after her lifetime.Smith is among two landowners in Upstate South Carolina who have recently protected more than 250 acres of family-owned land through conservation easements arranged with non-profit organisation Upstate Forever. The second property, Moore Farm, covers 110 acres in Greenville County and belongs to Ed Lomas's family.The organisation said the two agreements are part of its wider effort to protect land across the region. Upstate Forever now safeguards more than 40,000 acres across 10 counties.How conservation easements protect landA conservation easement is a legal agreement that allows property owners to retain ownership while placing permanent restrictions on development. These restrictions continue to apply even if ownership of the property changes.Scott Park of Upstate Forever said landowners grant these restrictions to the organisation, which takes responsibility for ensuring that the agreed protections remain in place."Conservation easements, they’re in essence a charitable donation, so that’s why Upstate Forever can be a grantee of these conservation easements," Park said.He explained that the landowner grants the restrictions and the organisation becomes the long-term steward of the property."So the landowner is the grantor; they grant those restrictions to Upstate Forever. We are the forever steward, so we’re almost a partner in the pocket of that landowner now for as long as that landowner owns that piece of property."Another family protects its century-old farmThe second property covered by the agreements is Moore Farm, owned by the Lomas family for more than 100 years. The 110-acre farm is located near Horsepen Creek in Greenville County.The property was previously used to grow cotton. Since around the 1950s, it has been used to raise cattle. However, new residential neighbourhoods have gradually developed around the farm.Ed Lomas said the change has been particularly noticeable in the traffic passing through the area. "Twenty years ago, you would wait for cars to come by maybe every few minutes," Lomas said. "Now it’s a constant stream, especially first thing in the morning."The process of securing the conservation easement took around a year and a half. Lomas said he decided to protect the farm after hearing about another family that was struggling to hold on to its property.He recalled receiving a call from a family friend whose relatives were getting older and could no longer manage their land. They were concerned about leaving the property to their children and the difficulties that could follow. "I actually had a phone call from a family friend about a year ago saying they had exactly that scenario," Lomas said.He said the family believed selling the property was their only option. "They were older, they couldn’t take care of it, it was going to be left to the children, it was going to be a big mess. They felt that was their only option, just to sell the land."Lomas wanted to prevent his own family from facing similar pressure. He said the agreement would protect the farm and ensure that his children would not be pressured into selling it for development. "I know it’ll be safe and the kids will not be able to be pressured into selling it as a development," he said.Conservation agreements offer tax benefitsConservation easements can also provide financial benefits to property owners because they are treated as charitable donations.According to the South Carolina Farm Bureau, the value of an easement is calculated by comparing the property's fair market value before and after the development restrictions are imposed. The difference is recognised by the Internal Revenue Service as a non-cash charitable donation. Landowners can claim this amount as a federal tax deduction for up to 15 years.South Carolina also offers state tax credits, generally amounting to a maximum of $250 per acre. These credits have no expiration date and can be applied towards the landowner's personal income.In addition, many easements qualify for direct financial support from sources such as the South Carolina Conservation Bank. This funding is generally calculated as a percentage of the easement's value and paid to the landowner at closing.Families want others to consider the optionPark said Upstate Forever was seeing growing interest from landowners who wanted to protect their properties against development.He said families such as the Lomas and Smith families were determined to preserve land that had remained in their families for generations."You meet landowners like Ed and Alice that are just salt of the earth," Park said. "They just want to protect their property. They see the development pressure that’s coming around them and they are pretty much, they are laser focused on getting these properties protected, and we’re happy to be a partner in that."Both landowners said they hoped their decisions would encourage other families to explore ways to protect their properties."There are opportunities and ways to protect and conserve the property you may have," Lomas said. Smith said she did not consider herself wealthy or well-connected but wanted others to know that protecting family land was possible."I’m not well-to-do, I’m not really well connected, but if for some reason I can plant a seed in anyone, that if I’m able to do this, they can too," she said.For Smith, the agreement means that her family's land will remain protected even after she is gone. She said she wanted to ensure that the work and sacrifices made by earlier generations were not lost to development."What your family sacrificed and worked so hard for did not go to waste and a developer is not going to be able to ever touch it, and even when I’m gone, it’s still going to stay like this," she said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Jesse and Kylie Sebero manage more than 500 acres of Wisconsin forest for both timber and wildlife and open it to researchers; they are among five families shortlisted for the state’s $10,000 Leopold Conservation Award
articles.summary: A forest can be both a source of timber and a home for wildlife when it is managed with conservation in mind.
articles.body: A forest can be both a source of timber and a home for wildlife when it is managed with conservation in mind. In Wisconsin, Jesse and Kylie Sebero are demonstrating how privately owned woodland can support economic activity while protecting natural habitats. The couple manages more than 500 acres of contiguous forest in Marinette County, balancing timber production with wildlife conservation. They also open their property to researchers and organise educational tours for landowners and forestry professionals.The Sand County Foundation announced on September 10, 2026, that the Seberos were among five finalists for the 2026 Wisconsin Leopold Conservation Award. The $10,000 award recognises farmers and forestland owners who make significant efforts to protect soil health, water quality and wildlife habitat while managing productive land. The foundation, which announced the shortlist, presents the award with national sponsor American Farmland Trust and state partners Wisconsin Farm Bureau Federation and Dairy Farmers of Wisconsin. The winner is scheduled to be announced on November 12.How the Seberos manage their 500-acre forestThe Sebero Family Tree Farm in Porterfield, Marinette County, covers more than 500 acres of contiguous forest. Rather than focusing only on timber production, the family considers the ecological and economic value of each acre.According to the Sand County Foundation, the Seberos manage the quality of timber and wildlife habitat across their property to achieve its fullest potential. Their approach reflects an effort to maintain a productive forest while ensuring that it continues to provide suitable habitat for wildlife. The family also makes the woodland available for research projects and tours. They welcome landowners, timber professionals and conservation experts who want to learn about forest management and conservation practices.Jesse Sebero's professional work further supports these efforts. He serves as a technical service provider for the US Department of Agriculture's Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS). In this role, he has written 272 forestry plans covering thousands of acres of privately owned land. His experience in providing technical guidance, together with the family's management of their own woodland, has made the Sebero property a place for research, learning and knowledge-sharing.Four other families shortlisted for the awardThe Seberos are competing with four other finalists whose conservation work focuses on farming, grazing, soil health and water protection. Andy Bensend of Dallas in Barron County has introduced cover crops, nutrient management and reduced tillage at AB Farms. Despite the shorter growing season in northern Wisconsin, he grows corn, soybeans and winter wheat while participating in research projects examining agricultural practices and soil health.The Brattset Family Farm in Jefferson County is managed by Weenonah Brattset and her daughter, Kirsten Jurcek. They have practised rotational grazing of beef cattle since 2005. Their work includes integrating cropland into perennial vegetation, improving soil health, water quality and biodiversity. They also work with the National Audubon Society to support grassland bird habitats and mentor other graziers.Jeff Endres, co-owner of Endres Berryridge Farms in Waunakee, Dane County, installed a manure composting facility to reduce the need for spreading manure during winter. He also founded the Yahara Pride farmer-led watershed group, which encourages farmers to adopt conservation practices and reduce phosphorus pollution in waterways.The Schoepp Family of Lodi, in Columbia and Sauk counties, uses no-till farming and diverse crop rotations to grow corn, soybeans, alfalfa and wheat. Their use of cover crops helps reduce soil erosion, improve soil structure and increase water infiltration. They also rotationally graze dairy heifers and beef cattle on cover crops.What is the Leopold Conservation Award?The Leopold Conservation Award is named after American conservationist Aldo Leopold, who promoted the idea of a land ethic in his influential 1949 book, A Sand County Almanac. His philosophy encouraged people to recognise their responsibility towards the land they own and manage. The award recognises farmers, ranchers and forestland owners who combine productive land management with efforts to improve the environment. Sand County Foundation and American Farmland Trust present the awards to private landowners across 28 states.In Wisconsin, the $10,000 award is presented with the support of the Wisconsin Farm Bureau Federation and Dairy Farmers of Wisconsin. An independent panel of agricultural and conservation leaders reviewed the applications and selected the five finalists. The first Wisconsin Leopold Conservation Award was presented in 2006 to woodland conservationist Gerry Mich of Appleton. The 2025 recipient was Michael Berg of Blanchardville in Lafayette County.The 2026 winner will be announced at the Wisconsin Board of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection meeting on November 12. For the Seberos, the nomination highlights how privately managed forests can serve several purposes at once, providing timber, supporting wildlife and creating opportunities for research and education.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nestlé to Astronomer: CEOs who lost their jobs over relationships with colleagues
articles.summary: The growing list of corporate chiefs losing their jobs over workplace relationships has once again raised questions about office romances and the risks
articles.body: The growing list of corporate chiefs losing their jobs over workplace relationships has once again raised questions about office romances and the risks they pose to companies. Nestlé CEO Laurent Freixe is the latest high-profile executive to face the consequences, after an internal investigation found that he had failed to disclose a relationship with a direct subordinate, violating the company's code of conduct.Nestlé said Freixe's departure followed an investigation into the undisclosed relationship. The company's internal reporting channel was reportedly used by employees to raise concerns about the matter. Freixe initially denied the allegations, Reuters reported."This was a necessary decision. Nestlé’s values and governance are strong foundations of our company,” chairman Paul Bulcke said in a statement announcing the leadership change.Nestlé has appointed Philipp Navratil, formerly the chair of its Nespresso division, as Freixe's successor.Freixe's exit adds to a growing list of corporate leaders who have lost their positions over relationships with colleagues, despite companies having policies to regulate or prohibit such conduct.Growing list of CEOs facing \consequencesWorkplace relationships have proved costly for several high-profile executives in recent years. In August, Andy Byron resigned as CEO of Astronomer after a viral video showed him with the company's chief people officer during a Coldplay concert.In May, Kohl's dismissed its former CEO Ashley Buchanan, just months after he took the job, over a romantic relationship with a woman whose coffee company did business with the retailer.In 2024, Norfolk Southern CEO Alan Shaw was forced out after having a consensual relationship with the company's chief legal officer.The list also includes former BP CEO Bernard Looney, who resigned in 2023 after failing to disclose several consensual relationships with colleagues. The same year, NBCUniversal CEO Jeff Shell was fired over an inappropriate relationship and allegations of sexual harassment.Former McDonald's CEO Steve Easterbrook was terminated in 2019 after having a relationship with an employee. Intel's Brian Krzanich was fired in 2018 after the company learnt about a past consensual relationship with a subordinate.Other cases include former Lululemon CEO Laurent Potdevin, who resigned in 2018, with a relationship involving a female designer reportedly among the issues behind his exit. Lockheed Martin's Chris Kabasik also resigned in 2012, before taking over as CEO, after an investigation revealed an affair with a subordinate.The consequences have not been limited to male executives. Nadine Ahn, former chief financial officer of the Royal Bank of Canada, was terminated in 2024 after an undisclosed relationship with a subordinate.Why office romances remain a concernRelationships between senior executives and their direct reports are particularly sensitive because of the power imbalance involved.Even when both individuals describe a relationship as consensual, it can be difficult to establish whether the subordinate felt free to make that choice. Such relationships can also raise questions about favouritism, conflicts of interest and whether professional decisions are being influenced by personal ties.This is why many organisations prohibit romantic relationships between managers and their direct reports. However, the rules do not appear to be preventing such relationships.A January 2025 Resume Genius survey found that 11% of Gen Z employees had been in a relationship with a direct report. The same percentage said they had been romantically involved with their boss.The actual number of workplace relationships could be considerably higher, as many remain undisclosed. A 2024 survey by the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) found that only 22% of employees involved in workplace relationships had disclosed them to their employers.Another survey in 2025 found that 86% of Gen X employees kept their workplace relationships secret.While some employees conceal relationships because their organisations prohibit them, others do so to protect their privacy. Relationships involving employees who are already married or committed to someone else can also remain hidden.Are companies getting their policies wrongThe growing number of such cases raises questions about whether outright bans are an effective way to deal with workplace relationships.One proposed alternative is to shift the focus from prohibition to transparency. Instead of relying primarily on disciplinary action, companies could provide confidential channels through which employees can disclose relationships.Such an approach would also require safeguards to prevent favouritism, monitor workplace decisions and ensure that relationships are genuinely consensual.Under this model, companies could avoid penalising employees simply for being in a relationship, provided they disclose it and comply with established ethical standards.However, implementing such policies is not straightforward. Employees involved in extramarital relationships may be unwilling to disclose them to their employers. Even where companies require disclosure, consensual relationship agreements, sometimes called 'love contracts', may not be used.It can also be difficult for organisations to distinguish between legitimate professional decisions and preferential treatment given to an employee's romantic partner.For now, companies continue to face the challenge of balancing employees' personal lives with professional accountability. Freixe's departure is the latest reminder that workplace relationships, particularly those involving differences in rank and authority, can have consequences that extend far beyond the individuals involved.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mexico arrests an alleged cartel leader wanted in the US and 19 others after a raid using DEA intelligence, with authorities linking the suspect to a mayor's killing and extortion of avocado producers
articles.summary: The lucrative avocado business in western Mexico has long been shadowed by threats, extortion and cartel violence.
articles.body: The lucrative avocado business in western Mexico has long been shadowed by threats, extortion and cartel violence. In one of the latest developments in the region's fight against organised crime, Mexican authorities have arrested an alleged drug cartel leader wanted in the United States, along with 19 other people, in an operation aided by intelligence shared by the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). The main suspect, Rafael "N", known by the alias "R2", is accused of leading a faction of the powerful Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) and has allegedly been linked to the killing of a local mayor who had spoken out against organised crime, as well as the extortion of avocado producers.According to Reuters, the operation took place in Zapopan, in the western state of Jalisco, on November 8. Mexico's Navy said its special operations unit carried out the operation in coordination with the country's security ministry, following intelligence work by Mexico's National Intelligence Center and information shared by the DEA. Nineteen other people were detained alongside R2.The arrest is significant because the suspect was allegedly a key figure in the "Los Rs" criminal faction, which operates across Jalisco and neighbouring Michoacan. Mexican Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said the group was involved in extortion, drug trafficking, homicide, kidnapping, unlawful detention and attacks on security personnel. Its alleged victims included business owners and avocado producers.Shootout during arrest operationThe arrest was not without violence. According to Mexico's Navy, its personnel came under armed attack during the operation and returned fire. R2 and one naval officer were wounded in the exchange and received medical attention. Authorities said the situation was brought under control.R2 had an outstanding arrest warrant in Mexico for aggravated homicide, as well as an arrest warrant connected to his extradition to the United States, Garcia Harfuch said. The DEA separately confirmed that he was wanted in the US on federal charges involving drug trafficking and firearms.Mexican authorities generally withhold the full surnames of criminal suspects in their official announcements, identifying them by their first name followed by "N". Consequently, the Navy's announcement identified the arrested man as Rafael "N", alias R2.Why is the suspect linked to a mayor's murder?One of the most serious allegations against R2 concerns the November 2025 killing of Carlos Manzo, the former mayor of Uruapan in Michoacan. The politician was shot dead during a public Day of the Dead celebration on November 1, while attending festivities with his family. Manzo, 40, had become known for openly challenging organised crime and demanding stronger action against the cartels operating in his municipality. Uruapan is a major centre of Mexico's avocado industry, and the surrounding region has repeatedly faced violence linked to criminal groups seeking control over agricultural businesses and transport networks.His killing shocked the country, particularly because it took place during a public celebration. A 17-year-old gunman shot Manzo, who later died in hospital. The attacker was subsequently killed by the mayor's security detail. Investigators believed other people had helped plan and facilitate the assassination.The investigation has since led to several arrests. In July 2026, Mexican authorities arrested another alleged Los Rs leader, Ramon Angel Alvarez Ayala, known as R1. Officials identified him as a suspected mastermind behind Manzo's assassination. R2's arrest is a separate development in the investigation and the wider crackdown on the faction. Following her husband's death, Manzo's wife, Grecia Quiroz, took over as mayor of Uruapan, pledging to continue his fight against organised crime.How avocado producers became cartel targetsThe allegations against Los Rs also draw attention to the criminal networks operating around Mexico's valuable avocado industry. Michoacan is one of the country's leading avocado-producing states, supplying domestic consumers as well as international markets. However, the industry's economic importance has made growers, transporters, traders and other businesses targets for organised crime.Cartels have allegedly used extortion, commonly referred to in Mexico as charging protection money, to extract payments from agricultural producers and businesses. Those who refuse to pay can face threats, kidnappings and violence. The criminal groups also seek influence over transportation routes and the movement of agricultural produce.Garcia Harfuch specifically identified avocado producers and business owners among the alleged victims of Los Rs. The group is also accused of involvement in drug trafficking, kidnappings and attacks on authorities across Jalisco and Michoacan.The pressure on agricultural communities has become a wider security concern. In October 2025, Bernardo Bravo, a prominent leader representing lemon producers in Michoacan, was also murdered. His killing highlighted the risks faced by agricultural leaders who speak out against extortion and organised crime.A wider crackdown on the cartel networkThe latest arrest comes amid an ongoing campaign by Mexican authorities against the CJNG, one of the country's most powerful criminal organisations. Its operations extend across several Mexican states, with networks involved in drug trafficking, extortion and violence.The DEA's intelligence contribution to the Zapopan operation also highlights cooperation between Mexican and US authorities in targeting suspects accused of operating across borders. While Mexican investigators are pursuing the homicide allegations and domestic criminal charges, R2 is also wanted in the US on federal drug and firearms charges.You use AI every day. articles.summary: The 24-year-old gunman who killed six people in a shooting at a historic square in Poland's Krakow on Saturday has died in hospital, police said early on
articles.body: The 24-year-old gunman who killed six people in a shooting at a historic square in Poland's Krakow on Saturday has died in hospital, police said early on Monday.The suspect was shot by police officers and arrested shortly after opening fire from his car at the city's Main Market Square. Very little information has been released about him, Reuters reported.The Polish government said the attacker, who was from Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, a town of nearly 60,000 people in southeastern Poland, may have been influenced by far-right ideology."There were many different emblems on the perpetrator’s clothing that have been partially examined and interpreted," Karolina Galecka, a spokesperson for the interior ministry, told radio TOK FM on Monday, as perReuters."These patches were associated with various motifs that are currently being analysed by specialists," she added, declining to provide further details while the investigation continues.What happened in Krakow?The gunman allegedly drove through the city's busy Main Market Square in military-style clothing before opening fire on pedestrians and other targets. The shooting left six people dead, including a British national, and 15 others injured.According to reports by the Daily Mail and The Independent, the suspect was armed with an AR-15-style assault rifle and drove a black Subaru through the square, firing at multiple locations. He was also reportedly wearing a bulletproof vest.Police shot and wounded him before taking him into custody. Officers later found additional weapons and ammunition inside his vehicle, according to the reports.Suspected far-right links under investigationInterior minister Marcin Kierwinski said preliminary findings suggested the suspect held radical and ultranationalist views."Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Kierwinski said at a news conference.Galecka's remarks about the emblems on his clothing came as investigators examined possible ideological links behind the attack.Neighbours, however, described the suspect as quiet and polite, saying they had not noticed anything unusual about his behaviour.In a separate development, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities had found the bodies of the shooter's parents and sister, with apparent gunshot wounds, at their family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski. articles.summary: Amazon is making another attempt to bring robots into people’s homes, years after its Astro robot struggled to gain traction.
articles.body: Amazon is making another attempt to bring robots into people’s homes, years after its Astro robot struggled to gain traction. The company has assembled a new team to work on a “new-to-world robot product,” according to a CNBC analysis of job postings, signalling that Jeff Bezos’ vision of household robots may not be over. For those unaware, Amazon first began exploring the idea in 2017, when Jeff Bezos, then the company’s CEO, directed a team of device executives to build a robot for consumers. The effort led to Astro, a $1,450 Alexa-equipped robot that made its public debut at Amazon’s September 2021 event. It could move autonomously around a home, recognise faces and serve as a mobile security monitor.However, Astro never became a widely available consumer product. It was sold to only a few thousand customers through an invite-only programme. Amazon also introduced a business version of Astro in 2023, but discontinued it less than a year later.Amazon’s new robot project said to be more ambitiousOver the past several months, Amazon has reportedly redeployed much of the team that worked on Astro and brought in an MIT roboticist for its new home robotics effort, according to LinkedIn profiles reviewed by CNBC. Job postings offer a glimpse into what the company may be developing. One engineering listing, which has since been removed, described a robot designed to navigate “dynamic home environments” and operate autonomously alongside family members.In March, Amazon acquired New York-based Fauna Robotics, the company behind Sprout, a 3.5-foot-tall humanoid robot. Fauna became part of Amazon’s newly formed Personal Robotics Group.The group includes employees who previously worked at Lab126, Amazon’s research and development unit responsible for products such as Kindle, Echo, Fire TV and Fire Tablet. A June job posting also hinted at the company’s ambitions, saying it wanted to “create robots that are not just functional, but delightful.”It remains unclear whether Amazon plans to adapt Sprout for household chores, companionship or other everyday tasks. An October job listing for a user experience designer sought someone to “define what it feels like to live with a Fauna robot.”Amazon spokesperson Brad Glasser told CNBC that the acquisition reflects the company’s “committed to tackling the challenges that can unlock the personal robotics category.”“Our goal is simple: make robots people actually want to live and interact with in everyday human spaces,” one job listing stated.You use AI every day. articles.title: The 2026 US elections produced the first Native American woman governor and senator, while women also won the Navajo and Seneca nation presidencies; at least 75 Native women and gender-diverse candidates won races
articles.summary: For generations, Native American women have fought to have their voices heard in a political system where representation has remained limited.
articles.body: For generations, Native American women have fought to have their voices heard in a political system where representation has remained limited. The 2026 US midterm elections have brought a significant change, with several Indigenous women securing historic leadership positions and dozens of others winning elections across the country.Among the biggest milestones, voters elected the first Native American woman governor and the first Native American woman senator. Women also made history in two tribal nations, with the Navajo Nation and Seneca Nation of Indians choosing their first women leaders. According to election figures reported by The Guardian, at least 75 Native women, non-binary and Two Spirit candidates won races across the country. The results mark an important moment for Indigenous representation in American politics, where access to voting and political participation has a long and difficult history.Deb Haaland and Peggy Flanagan break new groundTwo of the most significant victories came in state and federal politics. Deb Haaland, a citizen of Laguna Pueblo and former US Interior Secretary under President Joe Biden, was elected governor of New Mexico. Her victory makes her the first Native American woman to lead a US state. Haaland had previously made history in 2018 when she and Sharice Davids, a member of the Ho-Chunk Nation, became the first Native American women elected to the US House of Representatives. Her latest victory adds another milestone to a political journey that has helped increase Indigenous representation at the national level.Meanwhile, Peggy Flanagan, a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe and Minnesota's serving lieutenant governor, won the state's Senate race. She will become the first Native American woman to serve in the US Senate when she takes office in January. The significance of her victory is particularly striking considering that only four Native American men had represented their states in the Senate during its 237-year history. At her victory celebration in St Paul, Flanagan acknowledged the women who had supported her journey, saying, "I could not run for the US Senate without Native women. I could not exist in the way that I do without Native women."Two tribal nations elect women leaders for the first timeThe historic victories were not limited to state and federal elections. Two major tribal nations also chose women to lead them. Crystalyne Curley was elected to lead the Navajo Nation, becoming its first woman leader. The Navajo Nation is the largest tribal nation in the US by geographical area, covering approximately 27,000 square miles across parts of New Mexico, Arizona and Utah. Curley was already an important figure in Navajo politics. In 2022, she became the first woman to serve as speaker of the Navajo Nation Council. Her election as leader marks another significant step in her political journey.However, her campaign was not without challenges. Speaking to the Associated Press, Curley said women in Navajo politics often have to work much harder than their male counterparts. "As women, we have to work twice or triple as hard, especially within Navajo politics," she said, adding that she had faced sexist comments during her campaign. Meanwhile, Tina Abrams was elected president of the Seneca Nation of Indians in western New York. She will become the first woman to lead the nation in its modern history.Reacting to her victory, Abrams acknowledged the generations of Seneca women who had paved the way for her. She said she hoped her achievement would encourage younger women to imagine themselves in leadership positions in the future.At least 75 Native women and gender-diverse candidates winBeyond these headline-making victories, the 2026 elections also brought broader gains for Indigenous representation. According to Advance Native Political Leadership and the news organisation ICT, at least 75 Native women, non-binary and Two Spirit candidates won elections across the country. The election cycle also saw a record 363 Indigenous candidates contest local, state and federal positions. At least 180 of them won their respective races.Among the winners was Claire Valdez, a citizen of Ysleta del Sur Pueblo and a Democrat from New York, who will join Sharice Davids in the US House of Representatives. Another important development was the possibility of a second Native American woman entering the Senate. Mary Peltola, who is Yup'ik, was still awaiting the outcome of her closely contested Alaska race when The Guardian published its report. Her result remained undecided at the time.For many Indigenous women, seeing political leaders from their communities succeed has also made public office seem more accessible. New Mexico state senator Angel Charley, who is Laguna, Zuni and Diné, told The Guardian that seeing Haaland and Davids in national politics helped her imagine a future in public service.A long road from limited voting rights to political representationThese victories carry added significance when viewed against the history of Native American political participation in the US. Native Americans were not allowed to vote across the entire country until the 1960s, despite being citizens. Their representation in elected offices developed gradually over the following decades. One important milestone came in 1985, when Wilma Mankiller became the first woman elected principal chief of the Cherokee Nation.In 2018, Haaland and Davids broke another barrier by becoming the first Native American women elected to Congress. Two years later, Haaland made history again when Biden appointed her as the first Indigenous person to serve as a US cabinet secretary. New Mexico also took steps to strengthen Indigenous political participation. In 2023, it became the first and only US state to implement an updated Native American Voting Rights Act, giving tribes greater input into decisions involving polling locations and redistricting.For Haaland, the latest victory is about more than becoming the first Native American woman governor. It is also about showing people who have rarely seen themselves represented in positions of power that leadership is possible regardless of their background or financial circumstances. The 2026 results, therefore, represent more than a collection of individual election victories. From state government and the US Senate to tribal leadership, Native American women are entering positions that were once largely inaccessible to them. Their success is also creating new examples for younger generations who may now see public leadership as a possibility.
